the possible combinations (genotypes) of the opposite
gametes are given in the sU￿SqUares. The resulting
phenotypes can be written under the genotypes.

monk and he conducted breeding experiments on
garden pea (Pisum sativum) out of sheer interest.
His fmdings became a milestone in biology.

l. Many warietios were available in alternative forn)s
of a character.

true, i.e. pnjuced the same generation after
generation.
3. Peas are normally self-pollinated but self-
pollination could be prevented by removing
corresponding repr(￿UCtive parts (male part stamens
and the fenMle part carpels) of the flower and could
as well be cross.pollinated artificially.

3.12 MENDEL'S LAWS OF INHEIUTANCE
Mendel's generalizations of the results of
breeding experiments are summarised under three
laws:
l. Law of Dominance. Out of a pair of
contrasting characters present together, only
one is able to express itself while the other
remains suppressed The one that expresses is
the dominant character and the one

2. Law of Segregation (also called the law of
purity of gametes). The two members of a pair
of factors separate during the forn￿ri0n of
gametes. They do not blend but segregate or

fusion at the time of zygo* formation.
3 Law of Independent Assortment. When there
are two pairs of contrasting characters, the
distribution of the members of one pair into the
gamefes is independent of the distribution of
the other pair (as is seen in the production of
gametes of the Fi hybrid in dihybrid cross).
Application of Mendel's laws
(i) A knowledge of the basic Mendelian principles
gives us an idea about the new combinations
in the progeny of hybrids and enables us to
predict their frequency.
(ll) Such information is of great importance to both
plant and animal breeders for producing better
breeds.
(iii) New types of plants with new combinations
of useful characters can be produced by
hybridisation.
